extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / educated readers interested in method and science
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and practical prescriptions for investigating nature: start from clear first principles, deduce ordinary effects, verify by experiment, and communicate results for collective progress. Includes methodological heuristics (model worlds, mechanical analogies) and specific empirical recommendations (dissection, focus on common phenomena).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept only what is clear and certain
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept as true nothing that did not appear to me more clear and certain than the demonstrations of the geometers had formerly appeared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational rule for belief: only admit propositions with clarity and certainty comparable to geometric demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find first principles in the mind (foundationalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: First, I have essayed to find in general the principles, or first causes of all that is or can be in the world, ... and without educing them from any other source than from certain germs of truths naturally existing in our minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin inquiry by identifying self-evident basic principles (roots in reason/mind) before deducing further results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduce effects from causes
rubrics_metrics.description: In the second place, I examined what were the first and most ordinary effects that could be deduced from these causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demonstration from causes to effects as the principal mode of explanation: derive phenomena logically from identified first causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simplified/hypothetical model-worlds to avoid scholastic dispute
rubrics_metrics.description: I resolved to speak only of what would happen in a new world, if God were now to create somewhere in the imaginary spaces matter sufficient to compose one, and were to agitate variously and confusedly the different parts of this matter, so that there resulted a chaos ... and after that did nothing more than lend his ordinary concurrence to nature, and allow her to act in accordance with the laws which he had established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create idealized hypothetical scenarios (a 'new world') to simplify assumptions and reason cleanly, avoiding entanglement with prior authorities' disputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer notions natural to the mind and avoid obscure scholastic forms
rubrics_metrics.description: I even expressly supposed that it possessed none of those forms or qualities which are so debated in the schools, nor in general anything the knowledge of which is not so natural to our minds that no one can so much as imagine himself ignorant of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate concepts that are evident and natural to human understanding rather than relying on contested scholastic categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek universal laws valid across possible worlds
rubrics_metrics.description: I endeavored to demonstrate all those about which there could be any room for doubt, and to prove that they are such, that even if God had created more worlds, there could have been none in which these laws were not observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim at discovering necessary, universal laws of nature (not merely contingent facts) to ensure broad explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain many phenomena from a few principles
rubrics_metrics.description: By considering the concatenation of these laws, it appears to me that I have discovered many truths more useful and more important... I have pointed out what are the laws of nature; and, with no other principle upon which to found my reasonings except the infinite perfection of God, I endeavored to demonstrate all those about which there could be any room for doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for explanatory economy: derive a wide range of phenomena (heavens, tides, light, formation of bodies) from a small set of clear principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus deeply on a single phenomenon before generalizing
rubrics_metrics.description: I resolved to expound singly, though at considerable length, my opinions regarding light; then to take the opportunity of adding something on the sun and the fixed stars, since light almost wholly proceeds from them ... and finally on man, since he is the spectator of these objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate particular phenomena in depth (e.g., light) as a way to ground broader theorizing about related topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mechanical analogies and mathematical-style demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: The motion which I have now explained follows as necessarily from the very arrangement of the parts, which may be observed in the heart by the eye alone, and from the heat which may be felt with the fingers, and from the nature of the blood as learned from experience, as does the motion of a clock from the power, the situation, and shape of its counterweights and wheels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain biological and natural processes by analogy to machines and by appeal to arrangements and forces; prefer reasoning that yields necessary consequences like mathematical demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical verification by direct observation and experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: I advise those who are not versed in anatomy, before they commence the perusal of these observations, to take the trouble of getting dissected in their presence the heart of some large animal ... and to have shown to them its two ventricles or cavities ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corroborate theoretical claims with direct empirical demonstrations (dissections, observations of valves, feeling heat), and use experiment to confirm theoretical deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin experimental work with ordinary, common phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to make use only of what is spontaneously presented to our senses, and of which we cannot remain ignorant, provided we bestow on it any reflection, however slight, than to concern ourselves about more uncommon and recondite phenomena: the reason of which is, that the more uncommon often only mislead us so long as the causes of the more ordinary are still unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with commonplace, readily observable phenomena for experiments; postpone rare or recondite phenomena until the common causes are understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase experimentality as inquiry proceeds to particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: I remarked, moreover, with respect to experiments, that they become always more necessary the more one is advanced in knowledge ... when I wished to descend to the more particular, so many diverse objects presented themselves to me, that I believed it to be impossible ... unless we rise to causes through their effects, and avail ourselves of many particular experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As theoretical knowledge grows, make more and more particular experiments to distinguish and establish specifics (forms, species, mechanisms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate findings to promote collective progress
rubrics_metrics.description: I judged that there could be no more effectual provision against these two impediments than if I were faithfully to communicate to the public all the little I might myself have found, and incite men of superior genius to strive to proceed farther ... by informing the public of all they might discover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish and share experimental results and methods so others can build on them, coordinate efforts, and accelerate collective discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use practical aims (arts, medicine) as motivation for inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: For by them I perceived it to be possible to arrive at knowledge highly useful in life ... we might also apply them in the same way to all the uses to which they are adapted, and thus render ourselves the lords and possessors of nature ... and especially for the preservation of health ... I designed to employ my whole life in the search after so necessary a science [medicine].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drive natural-philosophical inquiry with practical applications (technology, medicine) to guide priorities and justify public dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish operations explainable by matter from those requiring a created soul
rubrics_metrics.description: I had described the reasonable soul, and shown that it could by no means be educed from the power of matter, as the other things of which I had spoken, but that it must be expressly created; ... it is necessary for it to be joined and united more closely to the body, in order to have sensations and appetites similar to ours, and thus constitute a real man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether a function (e.g., reason, sensation) is materially generated, consider whether mechanical/material explanations suffice; if not, posit a distinct principle (soul) — this is a metaphysical criterion for explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests for attributing thought or reason to a system
rubrics_metrics.description: Of these the first is that they could never use words or other signs arranged in such a manner as is competent to us in order to declare our thoughts to others ... The second test is, that although such machines might execute many things with equal or perhaps greater perfection than any of us, they would, without doubt, fail in certain others from which it could be discovered that they did not act from knowledge, but solely from the disposition of their organs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To judge whether an entity possesses reason: (1) can it use language/signs flexibly to declare thoughts? (2) can it display general, context-independent reasoning rather than fixed organ-driven responses?

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer explanations that yield practical, testable consequences (e.g., circulation, respiration, digestion)
rubrics_metrics.description: From these things ... the blood in the veins, flowing in this way continually into the heart, is not exhausted ... there are many small passages at the extremities of the arteries, through which the blood received by them from the heart passes into the small branches of the veins ... the true use of respiration is to bring sufficient fresh air into the lungs, to cause the blood ... to become thick, and to convert it anew into blood ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct theories that make clear, testable predictions about physiological processes; use observable interventions (ligatures, cutting arteries) as decisive evidence.
